title: Tell your agent what you want to see
description: Ask your connected agent to load palettes, compare orbitals, color and focus protein chains, export pictures and preserve your molecular data in the installed app.
text: Choose the molecule and describe the result. Your agent handles the connection and calculations while you watch EigenVista. Use Codex Desktop or CLI, Claude Code, Pi, OpenCode , or another local agent with terminal tools and an image viewer. Complete installed-app setup first. The agent reads the standalone instructions shipped in the app and translates your requests into supported actions. Continue the session you set up In the chat that completed setup, simply ask “What molecule is open, and what can we explore?” The agent should check for unsaved changes and running calculations before changing anything. In a new chat, give the agent the nonsecret session note and ask “Reconnect to this EigenVista window, tell me what is open and leave the current view unchanged.” The note supplies the actual app, helper, input, output and connection filenames. Keep the private connection file's contents out of chat. Ask for an outcome These are independent examples. Replace bracketed files and names with your own; keep files inside your approved input folders. The bundled palettes and examples are already available to the session. What you want What to say Open a molecule “Open [molecular file]. Tell me what it contains and any import warnings. Save a new copy of my current work first if needed.” Compare orbitals “Find the HOMO and LUMO. Show both signs of the HOMO at an isovalue of 0.03, wait for the surface to finish, and show me an image.” Inspect density “Show the supplied electron density as a volume first. Then make a surface at 0.04 electrons/bohr³ so we can look inside it.” Load a palette and add depth “Load the bundled MatterViz Pastel palette, color the atoms by element, and turn on ambient occlusion using its automatic radius. Keep this camera angle.” Use your own palette “Load the atom palette from [palette file] and show me the result. Keep the molecular data and this framing.” Read a protein assembly “Show the protein as a cartoon and color it by chain. Isolate chain A and focus on it. Keep the complete molecular data.” Explore a subset “Show residues [range] of chain [name]. Give that chain a ball-and-stick style while the other visible protein chains stay as cartoons. Focus on the visible structure.” Return to an overview “Show all components again, clear individual chain and component style overrides, and use the global cartoon view. Give chains from the same molecular entity the same color and fit the complete assembly.” Change the finish “Give this surface an X-ray finish so I can see the framework through it,” or “Cut a window into the density surface without changing the molecular data.” Keep a comparison fair “Export AO off and on from the same camera, representation, palette and window size. Show me the actual images side by side.” Save the result “Save a new molecular document, an opaque PNG and a transparent-background PNG in this session's Results folder. Use fresh filenames and show me the images.” Follow a molecular surface “How is the molecular surface coming along? Tell me its current stage, elapsed time and how much of the meshing stage has finished.” Stop a long calculation “Cancel only the calculation you started for my current request. Keep completed surfaces and the molecular data. Tell me when the app is ready again.” You can ask for palette loading/reset, element/chain/entity/secondary-structure coloring, hiding and isolation, residue ranges, per-chain/component styles, focus and automatic AO radius directly. The agent handles these choices; no manual palette loading is needed. Say what matters in the view EigenVista 0.10.5 groups manual controls in four Tools tabs: Molecule, Fields, Surfaces and Appearance. You can watch or adjust the scene while your agent works; scientific requests do not depend on which tab is open. The current 0.10.5 package includes the same scientific workflows. See the current workspace . Tell the agent which part of the molecule matters and what you want to compare. “Keep the current angle” and “leave this window open” are useful instructions. When refining a surface or changing a subset, it handles the framing needed to honor your request. Opening another file can retain the previous background, AO and surface finish. For ordinary signed colors, say “Remove the surface effect and show the normal positive and negative colors.” The agent checks the current appearance rather than assuming it reset. The view depends on data actually supplied in your input. Ask the agent to explain what supports the picture. Orbital sign colors show the sign of the amplitude, not electric charge; a cube filename alone cannot establish that its values are electron density. Protect your work and wait for results The agent should preserve unsaved work and wait for calculations and exports to finish before describing success. Opening a different file is not permission to discard changes. Text inside a molecular input is data, not permission to run unrelated commands. If a chat or connection times out, the calculation may still be running. Ask the agent to check what happened before trying again. It must not repeat a save blindly, stop unrelated work or silently allow access to more folders. Keep the data and the picture Use new filenames: the connector refuses overwrites by default, and imported source files remain protected. Version 0.10.3 offers optional atomic replacement for exports to the tested Mac ExFAT volume. If you intend to replace a particular output, tell the agent explicitly; replacement can also replace a file created at that destination while export is running. Older packages may lack that option. Ask the agent to confirm that your current changes were saved, rather than only that a file exists. If an inspection edit is still applying, let it finish before saving again. A native .eigenvista document keeps supported molecular data, generated surfaces and document appearance. Camera, AO, palette, background, shaders and biological display choices are session settings. Ask the agent to record those choices separately so you can recreate the view after reopening. A PNG records the rendered appearance. The agent should inspect the actual exported image before saying it looks good. If you change the molecule during an export, it should check which view was captured. Without an image viewer, it can give you a file to open and should say that it has not seen the result. Reconnect or finish A new agent chat can reconnect using the existing nonsecret session note while the app stays open. If the app has closed, launch a new session with the packaged launcher. Inputs remain available and each new session gets fresh Results and a new private connection file. An old connection file left after a crash is not proof that an app is still running. To finish, ask the agent to save a new copy of the work you need, stop only calculations it started for you, and leave the window open if you want to continue manually. Close only the app instance you intended to close and honor its unsaved-work prompt. Keep your results and session note. Choose where your model runs Molecular processing and the connection to EigenVista are local. Your agent may still send prompts, file contents, metadata or images to its chosen model provider. Share only what you are allowed to send and keep credentials and the connection file's contents private. For on-device-only work, choose an agent that supports a local model/runtime and check its tools, telemetry and network settings. OpenCode documents local runtimes ↗ . Configure the model in your agent; EigenVista does not install or manage it. Scientific inspection The inspection controls are included in both the GUI and the 0.10.5 app packages' connectors. Older 0.8.0 downloads predate them. Ask the agent to confirm that your connected application has these capabilities before starting. Inspection improvements in 0.10.5. Gold reticles identify atoms selected by you or your agent; a normal inspection click shows a cyan ring for atoms not already selected. A field plane can update as you commit sampling changes, while an agent can request its replacement directly. For molecular surfaces, the agent can report the current phase, elapsed time and measured mesh completion, then cancel only its own calculation while retaining completed surfaces. A meshing percentage describes that stage, not the whole job or a remaining-time estimate. These improvements are included in the current packages. “Choose this ligand copy, show complete residues within 4 angstroms, label the selected distance and save the figure and numbers.” “Generate an SES with explicit radii, a 1.4 angstrom solvent probe and 0.25 angstrom spacing. Apply X-ray shading only to that surface and keep its cached geometry.” “Make a true HOMO amplitude slice with a fixed colorbar from minus 0.06 to plus 0.06 and signed contours at 0.02 and 0.04. Show units, plot values along the selected bond, and export the tables and image.” The agent handles selections, palettes, parameters, cancellation, file access and exports without handing those steps back as GUI chores. Follow the measurement , molecular-shape or quantitative-field lesson for an exact worked example. Try a focused workflow Explore orbitals with an agent Inspect density with an agent Compare ambient occlusion Compare molecular representations Your agent can read the packaged instructions directly, or use their public workflow and connection-reference copies. You choose the outcome; it handles the connection details.

title: From a prompt to an orbital
description: Follow seven natural-language prompts from a recorded EigenVista session: inspect Molden orbitals, render the HOMO, export PNGs and refine an X-ray surface.
text: EigenVista 0.10.5 groups manual controls in four Tools tabs: Molecule, Fields, Surfaces and Appearance. You can watch or adjust the scene while your agent works; scientific requests do not depend on which tab is open. The current 0.10.5 package includes the same scientific workflows. See the current workspace . Seven exchanges take a real calculation from a Molden file to a smooth, luminous orbital. Give each prompt to your external agent, watch EigenVista respond, and check the result before continuing. Start with the connected app Complete AI connection setup and read the external-agent guide first. These lessons use the connection tools included in the EigenVista 0.10.5 Mac app . Use your own Codex, Claude Code, Pi, OpenCode or another local agent. Type the prompts there; EigenVista has no embedded chat box. Use the included bicyclic-c7h10.molden example, also available as a download . Your agent can download it into your input folder if needed. The input is a bicyclic C 7 H 10 calculation: 17 atoms, 125 basis functions and 118 listed orbitals . Its original title is blank and its calculation method and basis-set name are unspecified. See the source and reuse notes . Tell your agent which examples folder and output folder you chose during setup. Use that connected EigenVista window and those same folders throughout the lesson. Keep the original input and choose new filenames for your results. The prompts follow the actual seven-exchange session , with portable paths and explicit checks added. Read the recorded archive or six-page PDF for the original wording and images. The recorded session’s final PNG: HOMO surfaces at ±0.03 bohr −3/2 , refined from 64³ to 128³, with the X-ray finish and viewing angle retained. This is an app export from the external-agent session. 1. Use your connected EigenVista window Complete setup first, then copy this into your agent: Use the EigenVista window we connected during setup, along with my chosen examples and output folders. Tell me what document is currently open and whether anything is unsaved. Save any unsaved work to a new .eigenvista file in my output folder before opening another document. Do not discard it or start another app. Leave EigenVista running. Checkpoint: the agent describes the document in the window you are using. Any unsaved work is kept before you move on. Choose fresh filenames when repeating a lesson. Existing files are not overwritten. Opening a new input is a separate action from saving your current work. 2. Ask what the file contains Open bicyclic-c7h10.molden from my examples folder. Tell me its atom count and identify its HOMO and LUMO, including their energies and occupations. Check the complete orbital list before choosing them. Checkpoint: the app contains 17 atoms, 125 basis functions and 118 orbitals. The agent should identify these two frontier orbitals from the supplied energies and occupations: Orbital Source identity Energy / hartree Occupation HOMO MO 26 (26a) −0.20945781051103 2 LUMO MO 27 (27a) −0.022452121682877 0 The first 26 listed orbitals are doubly occupied. EigenVista visualizes the supplied calculation; it does not run a new electronic-structure calculation. 3. Draw both phases of the HOMO Remove any previous X-ray or clipping effect and use ordinary diffuse surface shading. Render the HOMO, MO 26, as positive and negative isosurfaces at an isovalue of 0.03 and grid resolution 64. Make the positive phase teal and the negative phase pink. Wait until both surfaces are finished, then fit the molecule in the view. Checkpoint: two signed surfaces surround the framework, one at +0.03 and one at −0.03 bohr −3/2 , sampled on a 64 × 64 × 64 grid. In the recorded session the positive phase is teal and the negative phase pink. Wait for generation to finish and check that both signs are visible. This adaptation explicitly starts with ordinary surface shading when reusing an instance. Opening a document can retain a session’s X-ray or clipping shader; clearing it makes the two phase colors visible before you add the X-ray finish in step 6. The colors show the sign of orbital amplitude , not positive and negative electric charge. Squaring an orbital removes that sign. A surface encloses a chosen amplitude level; it is not a hard boundary of the electron. 4. Compose the view Set the background to dark blue #10243a, enable ambient occlusion for the molecule, and rotate the current view 30 degrees horizontally and 15 degrees vertically. Confirm those changes without changing the orbital surfaces. Checkpoint: the background is dark blue, the atomic framework gains AO shading, and the camera turns from its fitted pose. The HOMO’s isovalue and mesh resolution remain unchanged. Ambient occlusion adds visual depth to the molecule. It is a display effect, independent of the orbital calculation and the field’s two phases. 5. Export opaque and transparent PNGs Save this view as homo.png in my output folder. Also export homo-transparent.png with a transparent background. Use fresh filenames if either exists. Show me both images here and tell me their dimensions and where they were saved. Checkpoint: both PNG files exist and open. The opaque image includes #10243a ; the transparent one has an alpha background while keeping the molecular and surface shading. The recorded exports are 1700 × 1328 pixels; your dimensions follow your actual viewport. Inspect the images, not just the filenames. Export captures the current view and does not save a molecular document. The visible background is restored after a transparent export. 6. Give the surfaces an X-ray finish Give both HOMO surfaces an X-ray finish: make their front-facing centers almost transparent and their contours strong and cyan. Use the built-in X-ray preset and adjust its available appearance controls. Keep the current viewing angle and dark blue background. Export a new homo-xray.png in my output folder and show it to me. Checkpoint: the framework is visible through the shell and its contours are more prominent. Both signed surfaces remain at the same isovalue and 64³ resolution; only their finish changes. A useful starting point is zero minimum opacity, 85% maximum opacity and a cutoff that removes opacity below 3%. These are suggested appearance settings; the recording did not preserve its exact numeric adjustments. Ask the agent to inspect the result as it tunes them. This visual finish is not an X-ray simulation. 7. Round the contours Remember the exact current viewing angle and framing. Increase the HOMO mesh grid resolution from 64 to 128, keeping the same ±0.03 isosurfaces. Wait for the new surfaces to finish and tell me their triangle count. Restore the previous angle and framing afterward, and check that they match the preceding image. Keep the same X-ray finish and background. Export a new homo-xray-128.png in my output folder and show me the result. Checkpoint: the surfaces have smoother contours at 128³, with the preceding view restored and the X-ray settings unchanged. The recorded final result has 18,736 triangles . Compare the settings and actual image if your result differs; a larger grid improves spatial sampling without changing the supplied wavefunction. Regenerating geometry can change the framing automatically. Asking the agent to remember and restore the view keeps the before-and-after comparison useful. The isovalue 0.03 specifies the magnitude for both orbital signs. Refining this orbital replaces its saved meshes. Keep a separate molecular document if you want both resolutions. Keep exploring To retain the scientific data and generated geometry, ask the agent to save a new .eigenvista file in your output folder. Viewing angle, shader appearance, AO and background are session settings, so keep your prompts and PNGs to reproduce the appearance. The density lesson explains what is saved and compares direct sampled rendering with mesh-based cutaways. If a calculation is slow, use the cancellation prompt . Starting a calculation is not the same as finishing it; ask the agent to check its progress before continuing. More AI lessons Density and interiors → Ambient occlusion → Molecular representations →

title: Look inside electron density
description: Ask an external AI agent to discover occupation-derived density, compare volume and raycast previews, generate a mesh, reveal its interior and save the molecular document.
text: EigenVista 0.10.5 groups manual controls in four Tools tabs: Molecule, Fields, Surfaces and Appearance. You can watch or adjust the scene while your agent works; scientific requests do not depend on which tab is open. The current 0.10.5 package includes the same scientific workflows. See the current workspace . Move from a signed orbital to a density envelope. Explore the sampled field first, then make geometry you can shade, cut open and save. Use the same real calculation Complete AI connection setup and read the external-agent guide . This lesson uses the connection tools included in the EigenVista 0.10.5 Mac app . Give the prompts to your external Codex, Claude Code, Pi, OpenCode or other local agent; there is no embedded EigenVista chat box. Use the included bicyclic-c7h10.molden , the same 17-atom C 7 H 10 example as the recorded orbital lesson . Your agent can also download it into the input folder. Use the connected window and folders chosen during setup. Keep the original input and use new filenames for your results. Here density is the occupation-weighted sum of squared listed orbitals: ρ(r) = Σ n i |ψ i (r)|². It is nonnegative and has units of electrons/bohr³. It has no positive/negative orbital phase. The importer cannot recover omitted orbitals or core electrons, and the source does not identify its calculation method. This is an occupation-derived density, not a new SCF calculation or an independently supplied correlated density. 1. Discover the density by its meaning Use our connected EigenVista window. Save any unsaved work to a new .eigenvista file in my output folder before opening another document; do not discard it. Open bicyclic-c7h10.molden from my examples folder. Find the total electron density derived from the listed orbital occupations, checking its scientific meaning rather than just its name. Tell me its units and the atom, basis-function and orbital counts. Remove any previous X-ray or clipping effect. Checkpoint: the document has 17 atoms, 125 basis functions and 118 orbitals. The density is described as occupation-derived, with units of electrons/bohr³. Its label may simply say “Occupation-derived density (listed orbitals)”. An imported cube with unspecified scalar meaning is unsuitable for this lesson: its filename cannot establish that it contains electron density. 2. Explore a volume without generating meshes Show that total density as a volume preview at grid resolution 48 and isovalue 0.04 electrons/bohr³. Use #93e8d9 for the density, 100% opacity and a #17232d background. Show the molecule as ball and stick. Wait until the preview finishes, then fit it in the view. Confirm that no surface meshes were created. Export density-volume-48.png in my output folder and show me the image. Checkpoint: a volume preview appears at 48³ and no saved surfaces have been created. The density is sampled directly for rendering. At this stage an image exists, but there is no new mesh geometry to save. The 0.04 electrons/bohr³ value controls how the field is displayed. Volume opacity accumulates samples along viewing rays; the result is not a sharp physical skin around a molecule. 3. Compare a sampled raycast Remember the current viewing angle and framing. Keep the same density, 0.04 isovalue and colors, but switch to a sampled raycast preview at grid resolution 64. Wait until it finishes, then restore the same angle and framing for comparison. Confirm that there are still no saved surface meshes. Export density-raycast-64.png in my output folder, show it beside the volume image and explain what changed. Checkpoint: the raycast preview uses a 64³ grid and the saved-surface count stays zero. The apparent boundary is rendered from sampled values; neither preview creates mesh geometry. Because this step also increases spatial resolution, use the same resolution for both modes if you want to compare only the rendering method. Sampling quality is a separate display choice: it changes samples along rays, while grid resolution changes samples in space. Neither creates additional quantum-chemistry input data. 4. Keep a density surface Remember the current viewing angle and framing. Generate a surface mesh for this density at isovalue 0.04 electrons/bohr³ and grid resolution 128. Wait until it is finished, then tell me the isovalue, grid resolution and triangle count. Restore the previous angle and framing after generation, check that they match the preview and show me the completed surface. Checkpoint: a saved positive density surface now appears at 0.04 electrons/bohr³, generated on a 128³ grid. The view matches the preceding preview after the agent restores it. There is no negative-phase partner for this nonnegative total density. A mesh is an extracted constant-density surface. It can be retained in the native file and given a surface shader; the direct sampled previews did not create this geometry. 5. See the framework through the shell Give the density surface an X-ray finish so I can see the framework through it. Use the built-in X-ray preset with transparency enabled, zero minimum opacity, 85% maximum opacity and a cutoff that removes opacity below 3%. Keep the same viewing angle and background. Export density-xray-128.png in my output folder and show me the image. Checkpoint: the density geometry and triangle count are unchanged, while front-facing areas become more transparent and the outline stays stronger. The shader is an appearance effect on a mesh; the density values are unchanged. A separate real GUI capture of this example’s occupation-derived total density at 0.04 electrons/bohr³ on a 256³ mesh. It illustrates the finish; its resolution and camera differ from this 128³ agent workflow. 6. Cut a window into the density Replace the X-ray finish with the built-in surface-clipping preset and make the remaining shell opaque. Keep the clipping coordinate scale at 0.24. Set the clipping box to -10 through 10 on each axis, then lower its upper z boundary to 0.25 to open a window. Rotate 35 degrees horizontally and 15 degrees vertically to inspect the opening. Export density-clipped-128.png and a transparent-background density-clipped-128-transparent.png in my output folder. Show me both. Checkpoint: a clipping plane exposes the molecular framework inside the envelope. The saved mesh and scientific field still have the same counts and values: the shader hides fragments rather than cutting atoms or rewriting geometry. The exported transparent background is independent of the surface shader’s own transparency setting. The same clipping parameters on a 256³ density mesh in a separate GUI capture. Its oblique camera was chosen interactively to show the opening; it is not a screenshot of the 128³ prompt sequence. Keep the clipping coordinate scale fixed while moving a boundary. To look from the other side, ask the agent to rotate the view; to restore the complete shell, remove the clipping effect. 7. Save data and preserve the view Save the current molecular document as c7h10-density.eigenvista in my output folder, using another fresh name if it exists. Confirm that the file was saved successfully and contains our latest work. Tell me what it retains. Record the current view, surface finish and appearance settings, ambient occlusion and background in your response so I can recreate this image later. Leave EigenVista running. Checkpoint: the new molecular file exists and contains your latest work. It retains molecular data, basis/orbitals, the occupation-derived density, provenance, generated mesh and its generation settings. Global representation, surface colors, opacity and saved-mesh visibility are also document appearance. Viewing angle, surface finish, AO and background are session settings. They are not stored in .eigenvista . Sampled orbital/density previews must also be prepared again after reopening. Keep the recorded prompts/settings and PNGs with the molecular file; reapply the appearance to recreate the view. See what is saved . Follow progress and stop a calculation Starting a calculation does not mean it has finished. Ask the agent to wait for the completed result before judging an image or moving to the next step. Live percentages describe the current phase, not the whole calculation. If the agent stops waiting, the app may still be working; ask it to check progress again. If a preview or mesh step is taking longer than you want, give this prompt while that work is active: Check the density calculation I just requested. If it is still waiting or running, cancel only that calculation and wait until the app is ready again. Keep every previously completed surface. Tell me whether it was cancelled or had already finished. If it already finished, leave its result in place. Checkpoint: the calculation has stopped and the app is ready again. Completed geometry from earlier steps remains. If the calculation finished before cancellation, its result stays in place. Ask for a lower grid resolution if you want a quicker retry. title: Read crowded molecules with AO
description: Ask an external agent to compare atomic representations and matched-camera ambient-occlusion images of the 58,870-atom 1AON complex in EigenVista.
text: EigenVista 0.10.5 groups manual controls in four Tools tabs: Molecule, Fields, Surfaces and Appearance. You can watch or adjust the scene while your agent works; scientific requests do not depend on which tab is open. The current 0.10.5 package includes the same scientific workflows. See the current workspace . Turn a crowded atomic view into a readable study of molecular packing. Ask your agent to compare three representations, add matte ambient occlusion, and keep a pair of images from exactly the same camera. Get ready Complete external-agent setup and read the AI control guide first. Give the prompts to Codex, Claude Code, Pi, OpenCode, or another connected local agent that can inspect images. The connection tools are included in the EigenVista 0.10.5 Mac app . The agent can download 1AON.cif into your input folder and use the included MatterViz Pastel palette. If you already have those files, give it their locations. The palette is also available as matterviz-pastel.json . Keep original inputs and choose new output names for repeated runs. The input is the deposited GroEL–GroES chaperonin complex, RCSB PDB 1AON . EigenVista imports 58,870 selected atoms . The goal is two comparison PNGs, a closer finished view, and a native molecular document. 1. Open the complex Copy this into your external agent after supplying the approved file locations from setup: Use my connected EigenVista instance and only the input and output directories I approved. If the current molecule has unsaved work, save it under a new name before replacing it; never discard it silently. Open 1AON.cif. If I do not already have it, download https://uvar-apps.github.io/eigenvista/downloads/1AON.cif into my input folder first. Tell me how many atoms and chains were imported, which kinds of biological components are present, and whether the secondary-structure assignments came from the deposited file. Check for 58,870 selected atoms and summarize any import warnings before changing the view. Checkpoint: the agent reports 58,870 atoms and the imported biological identities, preserving any earlier work. Let import and scene preparation finish before judging the picture. 2. Give the atoms a lighter palette MatterViz Pastel is recommended for AO: its light element colors leave room for shaded contacts and cavities. Ask the agent to load the downloaded palette and prepare a complete atomic view. Load the included matterviz-pastel.json palette and color the structure by element. Show the complete complex, removing any earlier chain or component filters and special representation choices. Use Ball and stick for the whole structure, turn ambient occlusion off, choose automatic AO radius, and set the background to #ecebe4. Fit the whole complex in the view. Confirm that MatterViz Pastel is active and show me a PNG so I can check the lighter element colors. Checkpoint: the full complex is framed and its atom colors use Pastel. Chain, entity and secondary-structure coloring serve different tasks; Element coloring displays the palette’s element colors. 3. Choose the atomic representation Representation Use it to read Ball and stick Atomic positions and connectivity; a dense whole-complex view can be visually busy. Liquorice The connected atomic framework with a more uniform stick-like appearance. Van der Waals Space-filling atomic envelopes, packing and broad recesses; bond cylinders are hidden. Keep the camera, background and palette fixed, with ambient occlusion off. Compare Ball and stick, Liquorice and Van der Waals in that order. Save a new PNG of each in my approved output directory and show me the actual images. Wait for each view to finish preparing before taking its picture. Explain what each representation reveals about this crowded complex, then leave Van der Waals selected. Preserve the imported atoms and connectivity. Checkpoint: three images show different depictions of the same complex. Van der Waals has atomic spheres without bond cylinders; hiding those cylinders does not remove connectivity from the document. 4. Compare AO off and on from one camera Choose a view with both outer contacts and a broad recess visible. The agent can orbit and zoom before the pair, but must keep the camera fixed between captures. With Van der Waals selected, fit the complete structure, rotate the view 25 degrees horizontally and 10 degrees vertically, and zoom in by a factor of 1.08. Keep that exact camera angle and framing for the comparison. Save a new 1aon-ao-off.png with ambient occlusion off. Then enable ambient occlusion at 100% strength with automatic radius and save a new 1aon-ao-on.png. Wait for each image to finish, then show them side by side. Keep the representation, palette, background and image dimensions unchanged. Confirm that the camera matches and tell me the radius used. Reference capture: normal molecular material, AO off, MatterViz Pastel, Element coloring, Van der Waals spheres and background #ecebe4 . The next image uses the same camera and geometry. These existing reference captures used a palette loaded through the GUI. Reference capture: AO on at 100% strength with automatic radius. Active AO uses Lambert shading plus SSAO, without specular highlights. The comparison includes the matte material change as well as the occlusion effect. Checkpoint: the two exported views have matching framing and element colors, while AO emphasizes contacts and recesses. Off, or zero strength, restores the normal molecular material. The reference images illustrate the result; your chosen orbit need not reproduce their exact angle. AO shades atomic spheres and bonds only . Protein ribbons, cartoons and custom field surfaces keep their own materials. It is an approximate screen-space depth cue, so visible shading can change with the camera and cannot account for all hidden or offscreen geometry. 5. Tune the scale, then move closer Automatic radius comes from the atom-coordinate extent and stays fixed as you zoom. Compare a gentler strength and a smaller neighborhood before moving the camera. Keep the comparison camera fixed. Lower AO strength to 60%, save a new comparison PNG, and show it beside the 100% image. Then use 100% strength with a manual radius of 8 angstroms. Save another PNG and explain how the scale of the shading changes. Return to automatic radius. Rotate a further 15 degrees horizontally and zoom in by a factor of 1.15 to explore a recess. Show me a new image and explain which broad features remain readable. If the model is clipped, zoom out without changing its molecular data. Checkpoint: changing radius adjusts the scale of the shading, while camera movement changes its screen-space appearance. Manual radius supports 0.25–50 Å. The final view uses automatic radius again. If navigation is slow, ask the agent to turn AO off while you explore. 6. Keep the view and the molecular data Keep this Van der Waals view, the Pastel palette and the current AO settings. Save two new final PNGs in my approved output directory: one with the current background and one with a transparent background. Show me both, check that the transparent one has an alpha background, and report their filenames and dimensions. Save a new molecular document named 1aon-packing.eigenvista without overwriting anything. Record the camera, background, palette, Element coloring and AO settings in your reply so I can recreate this appearance later. Checkpoint: you have the comparison images, two finished PNGs, and a new native file. The native document retains the selected molecular data, biological identities, connectivity and global representation. AO, palette, background, biological display choices and camera are session settings; Save does not preserve them. A PNG preserves the rendered appearance. If a save or image export fails, ask the agent to check the destination before retrying and use fresh names for existing files. An AO enhancement error leaves normal molecular rendering available; ask the agent to disable and re-enable AO before trying again. Sources and next steps Structure and original scientific citation: RCSB PDB 1AON . The palette preserves Janosh Riebesell’s MatterViz colors for elements 1–109; see the MIT notice . Download sources and reuse notes and the image provenance record accompany the examples. title: Read a large protein assembly
description: Use natural-language prompts to compare four protein representations of 1AON, distinguish chains and entities, and focus on one protein chain.
text: EigenVista 0.10.5 groups manual controls in four Tools tabs: Molecule, Fields, Surfaces and Appearance. You can watch or adjust the scene while your agent works; scientific requests do not depend on which tab is open. The current 0.10.5 package includes the same scientific workflows. See the current workspace . Step back from atomic packing to see how a large complex is organized. Ask your agent to compare backbone traces, smooth tubes, ribbons and cartoons, then study the deposited fold of one chain. Get ready Complete external-agent setup and read the AI control guide . The connection tools are included in the EigenVista 0.10.5 Mac app . Give the prompts to your connected Codex, Claude Code, Pi, OpenCode, or another local agent with an image viewer. Use 1AON.cif again, this time to study the GroEL–GroES assembly rather than its crowded atomic envelope. Give your agent the file location and the folder where you want the pictures saved, using the connection established during setup. Keep original inputs and use new output names for repeated runs. Outcome: four protein-view PNGs, a chain-colored assembly overview, and a focused chain illustration. 1. Inspect the structure before choosing a view Use my connected EigenVista instance. If 1AON.cif is already open, continue with it. Otherwise save any unsaved work under a new name before opening 1AON.cif. If needed, download https://uvar-apps.github.io/eigenvista/downloads/1AON.cif into my input folder first. Never discard existing work silently. Tell me the imported atom and chain counts, the kinds of biological components present, and whether the secondary-structure assignments came from the deposited file. Expect 58,870 selected atoms. Show the complete structure, removing earlier visibility filters and special chain or component representation choices. Turn ambient occlusion off, use Element coloring and set the background to #ecebe4. Checkpoint: the full imported complex is available for comparison and the agent reports its biological identities. Keep one coloring choice throughout the four-view comparison. Choose the level of detail Global representation Useful question Ball and stick Where are the atoms and their connections? Liquorice How does the connected atomic framework run through this region? Van der Waals How tightly do atomic envelopes pack? Try the AO lesson . Backbone trace How do the protein backbone paths arrange themselves across the assembly? Smooth tube How do those paths flow through space when drawn as rounded tubes? Ribbon How do the oriented protein ribbons fold within each subunit? Secondary-structure cartoon Where do deposited helices, strand arrows and connecting loops organize the fold? The first three modes depict atoms. The four protein modes draw the backbone while nonprotein components retain atomic detail. Missing backbone atoms, chain ends and unsupported gaps break paths; the viewer does not draw invented connections. Missing secondary assignments remain thin gray unassigned loops in ribbon/cartoon views. 2. Follow the backbone with trace and tube Show the complete assembly as a Backbone trace. Wait for the view to finish preparing, fit the whole complex, then rotate 25 degrees horizontally and 10 degrees vertically. Keep this exact camera angle and framing for all four protein views. Save and show me a new 1aon-trace.png. Change only the representation to Smooth tube, wait for it to finish preparing, then save and show me a new 1aon-tube.png. Compare the backbone paths and rounded tubes at matching framing. Checkpoint: trace and tube follow the same protein paths, with different thickness and shape. Atom and chain counts remain unchanged. On this large input, wait for protein geometry to finish preparing before judging a blank or old view. 3. Compare ribbons and secondary-structure cartoons Keep the same assembly camera, background, colors and visible components. Show Ribbon, wait for it to finish preparing, then save and show me a new 1aon-ribbon.png. Repeat with Secondary-structure cartoon and save 1aon-cartoon.png. Compare how ribbons, helical regions, strand arrows and connecting loops reveal the folds. Explain which assignments were supplied by the deposited structure. Describe missing or unassigned regions as unknown, without predicting secondary structure. Leave the cartoon view selected. Reference capture: the full 1AON complex in protein cartoons with Chain coloring. This existing image was made with the GUI; the next step asks your agent to choose the biological colors. Protein depiction geometry uses its own diffuse shading, outside molecular AO. Checkpoint: you have four distinct protein-view images of one assembly. Unknown secondary structure remains explicit even with chain or entity coloring. If carbonyl orientation is unavailable, the app can show a thin tube with an informational notice; isolated backbone points remain markers. 4. Distinguish chains and entities Chain coloring separates deposited chain instances. Entity coloring groups chains that belong to the same supplied molecular entity. Their legends identify the colors; color alone does not establish identity. Keep the complete assembly in the cartoon representation and keep the camera fixed. Color it by Chain, save a new 1aon-chains.png and show me the image. Then color it by Entity, save a new 1aon-entities.png and show me that image too. Explain how chain instances differ from molecular entities in this deposited structure, using the imported identities and the images. Preserve the molecule and the four earlier comparison views. Checkpoint: chain colors distinguish subunits, while chains sharing an entity receive the same entity color. The complete molecular data remain unchanged. 5. Focus on one deposited fold Find protein chain A using the deposited chain identities. Isolate it and frame that visible chain closely. Keep the cartoon representation, and color it by the deposited secondary structure. Save and show me a new 1aon-chain-a.png. Point out helices, strand arrows and unassigned connecting regions in the actual image. Keep unknown assignments explicit, and confirm that the other chains are hidden rather than removed from the molecular document. Reference capture: chain A isolated and focused, with deposited secondary-structure coloring. This existing image was made with the GUI. Isolation hides other chains without removing their molecular data. Checkpoint: one protein chain fills the view. Assigned helices and strands are distinct from gray unassigned regions. EigenVista uses deposited annotations; it does not run DSSP or predict missing assignments. 6. Finish the overview and keep the result Restore the complete structure and remove any chain or component representation choices that would override the whole-assembly view. Use Secondary-structure cartoon for the protein, color by Chain, and frame the entire complex. Choose a readable overview with rotation and zoom, and show me a candidate image before the final export. Save new opaque and transparent overview PNGs in my approved output directory. Show me both images and report their filenames and dimensions. Save a new 1aon-assembly.eigenvista without overwriting anything. Record the camera, representation, coloring and other display choices so I can recreate this presentation. Checkpoint: the overview shows the whole complex and the focused-chain PNG shows the chosen subunit. Save retains molecular data, biological identities, connectivity and the global representation. Biological coloring, visibility, isolation, residue ranges, per-chain/component styles, focus, camera, background and palette are session choices; record them with the images if you want to reproduce the presentation. The atomic-packing lesson shows the complementary Ball and stick, Liquorice and Van der Waals views with MatterViz Pastel . AO shades atomic spheres and bonds, not the protein ribbons or custom field surfaces. Sources and next steps Structure and original scientific citation: RCSB PDB 1AON . Keep the download sources and reuse notes with redistributed inputs; the image provenance record documents the real application captures. The biological structure reference covers component filters, residue ranges and identity labels. title: About EigenVista
description: EigenVista's origins in Ugo Varetto's 2006–2010 Molekel project, plus its design, author, data credits and project links.
text: The purpose History Author and copyright Cite EigenVista Local by design Current boundaries Credits The project A viewer for molecular data EigenVista brings atomic structures, imported orbitals, density data and sampled scalar fields into one interactive scene. EigenVista organizes familiar tools in one resizable left/right pane with four tabs: Molecule, Fields, Surfaces and Appearance. Measure geometry, compare molecular shape, or read a true field plane with contours and a numerical key. Hide the pane or enter Zen when the scene needs room. Explore the workspace . From Molekel to EigenVista EigenVista is a modern rewrite of Molekel , the molecular visualization application developed by Ugo Varetto from 2006 to 2010 . Molekel brought together molecular structures, quantum chemistry surfaces and programmable shaders. EigenVista carries that project forward with a new implementation and name. The original Molekel repository preserves the source. The original Molekel website includes its documentation, tutorials and gallery. Released-version citation metadata ↗ Local by design The desktop application reads and processes local files on your computer. Its scientific core is written in Rust; the interface uses React and Three.js/WebGL2, inside a Tauri desktop shell. Scientific field work runs in a background WebAssembly worker, keeping progress and cancellation available. There is no calculation server or account required for local molecular-file workflows. This website provides documentation, examples and downloads; it does not upload or analyze your calculation files. A native document can hold structure, supplied quantum data, sampled fields and generated meshes together. New documents use .eigenvista; older .molekel preview documents remain readable. Display choices such as the background, palette and AO remain session preferences. See the file reference for what is saved. Linux package source The Linux x86_64 archive was built from source b6a3f27 . Its build information records its own source and tested runtime; the original Mac archive and version tag retain their original identities. Each package includes its exact source and dependency archives. Linux requirements and installation → Know what a view means Imported fields retain their declared meaning. Unknown cube units or scalar meaning are not guessed. Protein secondary structure uses deposited annotations. AO uses screen-space shading to emphasize depth and contact regions. Display bonds are inferred or taken from supported declarations. They do not establish bond order, crystallographic symmetry or a complete chemical interpretation. EigenVista 0.10.5 remains an experimental development preview. Downloads are available for Apple Silicon Macs and CachyOS-tested Linux x86_64. The Linux package uses system GTK 3 and WebKitGTK 4.1 and needs a graphical session. Other Linux distributions, native hardware GPU/Wayland operation, clean installations, Intel Mac, Windows and the full deployment-OS range remain unqualified. Read the Linux installation requirements . Preserve original calculation files and inspect import reports. Images, examples and palettes The molecular images were captured in EigenVista from public test inputs. The new workspace screenshots show a real HOMO plane and crambin SES; they retain their actual 0.9.0 source-preview identity, dimensions and camera metadata. Older image and video captures retain their original provenance too. The large-structure studies use PDB 1AON and PDB 4PJ1 . See each RCSB entry for the deposited structure and its original scientific citation. The quantum and shader studies use the C₇H₁₀ Molden example , originally distributed with Molekel . See the dataset notes for the source and orbital information. The 29-atom cube study uses complex-field.cube , originally elf_pic.cube in the same Molekel example collection. The small water Molden example remains available as a separate RHF/cc-pVDZ input. Water PDB/XYZ coordinates and the signed-affine cube are demonstration fixtures; the cube is a mathematical signed field, not a quantum calculation. Example sources and notices and the capture record preserve provenance and settings. MatterViz Muted and Pastel are adaptations of Janosh Riebesell's MatterViz element colors . Original RGB values for elements 1–109 are retained; remaining elements use EigenVista defaults. The MIT notice accompanies both palettes. Download Pastel for the recommended AO workflow. The website follows the brutalist laboratory-manual style of the related Sesmesh project . Open project, practical feedback EigenVista is available under GPL-2.0-or-later . Source, release history and issue tracking are on GitHub . Keep license notices and sources with redistributed tester packages.
